title: SecVulEval: Context-Aware Benchmarking of LLMs for Vulnerability Detection
venue: Proceedings of the 3rd ACM International Conference on AI-Powered Software
design: Benchmark construction + empirical evaluation of 5 LLMs in a multi-agent detection pipeline (manual statement-level judging)
dataset: SecVulEval (NVD C/C++ CVEs 1999-2024, 707 projects, 145 CWEs); detection evaluated on 300-function subset from Top-25 CWEs
sample_size: 25,440 functions (10,998 vulnerable / 14,442 non-vulnerable; 5,867 CVEs); detection experiment 300 functions (~120 vulnerable)
metrics: Precision, recall, F1 at function level and statement level (statement TP requires correct reasoning); context-identification accuracy
main_finding: Best LLM (Claude-3.7-Sonnet) reaches only 23.83% statement-level F1 on real C/C++ CVEs; function-level F1 at most 53.89%; no static or DL baselines.

title: Revisiting the Performance of Deep Learning-Based Vulnerability Detection on Realistic Datasets
design: Replication + re-evaluation of 4 DL detectors (and 2 fine-tuned LLMs) on a new whole-project, time-split dataset (Real-Vul)
dataset: Real-Vul (C/C++, top-10 Big-Vul projects, full-codebase snapshots, temporal split); SARD, Big-Vul, ReVeal, IVDetect for replication
sample_size: 5,528 vulnerable functions (4,418 train / 1,110 test) + 1,682,713 uncertain functions (769,464 / 913,249)
metrics: Accuracy, precision, recall, F1, AUC; per-CWE-cluster and per-severity F1
main_finding: On whole-project realistic test data, DL detectors' precision falls to 1-10% (drops up to 95 pp) and F1 by up to 91 pp; fine-tuned LLMs trail LineVul on AUC.

title: Open or Frontier? A Cost- and Energy-Aware Benchmark of Large Language Models for Software Vulnerability Detection
design: empirical benchmark; zero-shot prompting of 8 LLMs (3 frontier, 5 open-weight) vs 3 SAST tools and 2 CodeBERT detectors on identical functions; cost/energy measured or estimated
dataset: PrimeVul test split (C/C++; 24,788 functions, 549 vulnerable, 1:44); stratified sample of all 549 vulnerable + 1000 safe functions
sample_size: 1549 functions (549 vulnerable, 35.4%); 8 LLMs x several configurations; 3 prompts; 3 safe-pool draws
metrics: balanced accuracy (primary), MCC, F1, recall, specificity, precision at 1:44 prevalence, FP/TP, USD/task, J/task, USD and kJ per true positive, latency
main_finding: Open LLMs dominate frontier on cost/energy; fine-tuned CodeBERT beats all LLMs (BA 0.765 vs ≤0.711); LLM precision at 1:44 prevalence 2.3–4.6% across two epochs.

title: Vulnerability Detection with Code Language Models: How Far are We?
venue: 2025 IEEE/ACM 47th International Conference on Software Engineering (ICSE)
design: Dataset audit (label accuracy, duplication) + new benchmark (PrimeVul) + empirical evaluation of 7 code LMs incl. GPT-3.5/GPT-4
dataset: PrimeVul (C/C++, merged BigVul/CrossVul/CVEfixes/DiverseVul, de-duplicated, temporal split); BigVul for comparison
sample_size: PrimeVul 6,968 vulnerable + 228,800 benign functions (755 projects, 140 CWEs); test 695 vuln/25,216 benign; 564 test pairs for GPT models
metrics: Accuracy, F1, VD-S (FNR at FPR<=0.5%), pair-wise P-C/P-V/P-B/P-R
main_finding: StarCoder2 F1 drops from 68.26% (BigVul) to 3.09% (BigVul-trained, PrimeVul test); best LLM (GPT-4 CoT) pair-wise correct 12.94%, below random 22.70%.

title: Reducing False Positives in Static Bug Detection with LLMs: An Empirical Study in Industry
venue: Proceedings of the IEEE/ACM 48th International Conference on Software Engineering: Software Engineering in Practice
design: Industrial empirical study at Tencent: interviews + offline evaluation of LLM prompting, hybrid LLM+static-analysis and DL methods for SAT alarm triage
dataset: 433 alarms from Tencent's proprietary SAT BkCheck on AMS codebases (mostly C/C++), Sep 2024-Jun 2025; NPD, OOB, DBZ bug types; confidential
sample_size: 433 alarms (328 FP, 105 TP); 5 interviewees
metrics: Accuracy, precision, recall, F1 (real bug = positive); FPR_P / FPR_R (precision/recall on false alarms); time and USD per alarm
main_finding: Hybrid LLM4PFA removes 94-98% of false alarms (recall of real bugs 0.75-0.88) at $0.0025-$0.12 per alarm; prompting-only and DL baselines are far weaker.

title: CASTLE: Benchmarking Dataset for Static Code Analyzers and LLMs Towards CWE Detection
design: Benchmark paper; 13 static analyzers + 2 formal verification tools vs 10 prompted LLMs on new hand-written C micro-benchmarks
dataset: CASTLE: 250 compilable C programs (7-164 lines), 25 CWEs, 6 vulnerable + 4 clean per CWE, line-level labels
sample_size: 250 programs (150 vulnerable, 100 non-vulnerable), 10,392 lines total; 25 tools/models
metrics: TP/TN/FP/FN, precision, recall, accuracy, new CASTLE Score (severity-weighted, FP-penalised), combination score
main_finding: On small C programs, top LLMs (GPT-o3-mini 977, o1, R1, GPT-4o) outscore all SAST and formal tools; best non-LLM ESBMC 661, CodeQL 634.

title: ChatGPT for Vulnerability Detection, Classification, and Repair: How Far Are We?
design: Short empirical comparison; prompted ChatGPT (gpt-3.5-turbo, gpt-4) vs fine-tuned code LMs on four vulnerability tasks
dataset: Big-Vul (C/C++, random 80/10/10 split); Big-Vul+CVEFixes repair pairs (Chen et al.)
sample_size: ~188k C/C++ functions (Big-Vul) + 5.5k repair pairs; number of functions actually sent to ChatGPT not reported
metrics: F1, precision, recall, top-10 line accuracy, multiclass accuracy, MSE/MAE, %PP, BLEU, METEOR
main_finding: Prompted gpt-4 reaches F1 29% (gpt-3.5: 10%) vs fine-tuned AIBugHunter 94% on Big-Vul; ChatGPT worst on all four tasks.

title: Large Language Models Versus Static Code Analysis Tools: A Systematic Benchmark for Vulnerability Detection
design: Head-to-head benchmark, 3 SAST tools (SonarQube, CodeQL, Snyk Code) vs 3 prompted LLMs (GPT-4.1, Mistral Large, DeepSeek V3)
dataset: 10 small author-prepared C# projects with seeded vulnerabilities (SQLi, XSS, secrets, command injection, weak crypto, outdated deps)
sample_size: 10 projects, 63 vulnerabilities, 3-10 files and 3,145-5,317 characters per project; single run per tool
metrics: Precision, recall, F1 (per-project, macro-averaged), false-positive ratio, execution time
main_finding: LLMs reach mean F1 0.75-0.80 vs 0.26-0.55 for SAST, driven by recall; LLMs mislocate lines and hallucinate outdated dependencies.

title: RepoAudit: An Autonomous LLM-Agent for Repository-Level Code Auditing
design: tool paper with empirical evaluation; LLM agent vs industrial static analyzers (Meta Infer, Amazon CodeGuru) and LLM baselines (CoT prompting, LLMDFA); ablations; model/temperature variation
dataset: 15 C/C++ benchmark projects from prior bug-detection papers (NPD, MLK, UAF; avg 251 KLoC) + 9 further open-source projects
sample_size: 15 benchmark projects (21 previously reported bugs); 9 additional projects; 3 bug types
metrics: TPs, FPs, precision; recall = share of 21 known bugs reproduced; prompts, input/output tokens, USD and seconds per project
main_finding: RepoAudit (Claude 3.5 Sonnet) finds 40 TPs/11 FPs (78.43% precision) on 15 projects at $2.54 and 0.44 h each; Infer 7 TPs, CodeGuru 0 TPs.

title: A Systematic Literature Review on Detecting Software Vulnerabilities with Large Language Models
venue: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
design: Systematic literature review (Kitchenham guidelines) with taxonomy and dataset analysis; descriptive mapping, no performance meta-analysis
dataset: IEEE Xplore, ACM DL, arXiv (search Dec 2024 + continuous alerts) + snowballing; Jan 2020 - Nov 2025; 20 datasets characterised, 12 re-analysed for CWE coverage
sample_size: 263 primary studies (185 peer-reviewed, 78 arXiv preprints); 4,155 database hits
metrics: Study counts per taxonomy category; dataset size, % vulnerable, #CWEs, CWE-1000 pillar coverage, dataset usage/co-usage frequency
main_finding: LLM vulnerability detection is fragmented: mostly binary function-level C/C++ classification on noisy, leakage-prone, long-tailed datasets with inconsistent splits, so results are hard to compare.

title: Understanding the Effectiveness of Large Language Models in Detecting Security Vulnerabilities
venue: 2025 IEEE Conference on Software Testing, Verification and Validation (ICST)
design: Empirical study, 16 prompted LLMs x 3 prompts vs CodeQL (synthetic only) and DeepDFA/LineVul (CVEFixes C/C++)
dataset: OWASP Benchmark, Juliet Java, Juliet C/C++ (synthetic); CVEFixes Java and C/C++ (real-world); MITRE Top-25 CWEs
sample_size: 5,000 function-level snippets (1,000 per dataset, 500 vulnerable / 500 non-vulnerable), 25 CWEs, single run at temperature 0
metrics: Accuracy, precision, recall, F1; balanced accuracy per CWE
main_finding: LLMs are modest (best accuracy 62.8% avg); CodeQL beats LLMs on synthetic data; LLMs win some CWEs; LLM vs DL F1 near trivial baseline.

title: IRIS: LLM-Assisted Static Analysis for Detecting Security Vulnerabilities
design: Tool proposal + benchmark evaluation (LLM-inferred taint specs + CodeQL + LLM alert triage) vs SAST baselines; 7 LLMs; ablations
dataset: CWE-Bench-Java (new; 120 manually validated CVEs in real-world Maven Java projects; CWE-22/78/79/94) + 30 latest-version projects
sample_size: 120 vulnerabilities (one per project); 30 projects for new-bug search; 960 manually checked spec labels; 50 manually checked alarms
metrics: #Detected / detection rate; average false discovery rate (AvgFDR); average per-project F1; spec recall/precision
main_finding: IRIS+GPT-4 detects 55/120 vs CodeQL 27/120, AvgFDR 84.82% vs 90.03%; smaller LLMs add detections but mostly worsen FDR.

title: LLM-based Vulnerability Detection at Project Scale: An Empirical Study
design: comparative empirical study; 5 specialized LLM detectors + 2 general coding agents vs 4 SAST tools, controlled benchmark + real-world projects, FP root-cause taxonomy, cost measurement
dataset: controlled set of 265 known vulns (ReposVul C/C++; CWE-Bench-Java; JLeaks) across 8 CWEs; 24 real-world C/C++ and Java projects/modules
sample_size: 265 known vulnerabilities (110 C/C++, 155 Java); 24 projects/modules; 6,442 sampled warnings; 5,896 FPs classified; 355 manually coded reports
metrics: recall, precision (controlled); #warnings, sampled false discovery rate SFDR (real-world); tokens, USD, minutes per project and per warning
main_finding: General agents (Codex, Claude Code) reach highest recall; specialized LLM detectors and SAST tools have near-zero recall on some CWEs and 75-100% SFDR; LLM cost up to $1,248/project.

title: From Lab to Reality: A Practical Evaluation of Deep Learning Models and LLMs for Vulnerability Detection
design: empirical evaluation; within/cross-dataset DL training + temporally separated OOD test of DL and off-the-shelf open-weight LLMs
dataset: Juliet, Devign, BigVul, ICVul (train/test); VentiVul (new; Linux+Chromium CVEs disclosed from 2025-05-01) for OOD
sample_size: 4 DL models x 4 datasets; VentiVul 13,326 functions, 200 CVEs, 263 vulnerable-patched pairs; 4 LLMs x 3 prompts
metrics: Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1; CVE Detection Rate (CDR); Patch Pair Accuracy (PACC); t-SNE centroid distance
main_finding: LineVul F1 91-94.5 in-distribution falls to 4.39-6.87 on temporally separated VentiVul (all 8 DL configs 3.47-8.65); open-weight LLMs 0.79-5.36; all-positive chance ~3.87.

title: A Review of Source Code Vulnerability Detection Methods Based on Large Language Models: Models, Techniques, and Evaluation
design: narrative (non-systematic) literature review, single author; no search protocol or quality assessment
dataset: none (secondary); 32 cited references, 2019-2026
sample_size: 32 references (no stated corpus of primary studies)
metrics: none (qualitative synthesis; re-reports P/R/F1, VD-S, Top-k, Effort@Recall from cited papers)
main_finding: LLM gains on benchmarks are inflated by duplicates, label noise, random/temporal splits; evidence supports SAST-LLM-human complementarity, not replacement.

title: Top Score on the Wrong Exam: On Benchmarking in Machine Learning for Vulnerability Detection
venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Software Engineering
design: Literature survey (81 ML4VD papers) + manual expert labelling study + word-count classifier probe for spurious correlations
dataset: BigVul, Devign, DiverseVul (C/C++ function-level benchmarks)
sample_size: 300 vulnerable-labelled + 90 secure-labelled functions manually analysed (2 annotators); 81 surveyed papers
metrics: Label accuracy, share context-dependent, Cohen's kappa, F1 / accuracy of word-count Gradient Boosting
main_finding: Only 39-65% of vulnerable labels correct; all 151 truly vulnerable functions need external context; word counts alone give F1 0.86 on BigVul (SOTA 0.96).

title: LLMs in Software Security: A Survey of Vulnerability Detection Techniques and Insights
design: Narrative (non-systematic) survey with keyword-driven, iterative venue search; no quality assessment; descriptive counts, no meta-analysis
dataset: Top security/SE venues (S&P, USENIX Sec, CCS, TSE, ...) + keyword searches; databases not reported; 2019-2024
sample_size: 58 highly relevant studies (from ~500-600 screened; >80 papers discussed)
metrics: Counts/shares of models, languages, techniques across studies; catalogue of 42 datasets (Table 4); per-study F1 listing (Table 5)
main_finding: LLM vulnerability detection research is mostly function-level C/C++ snippet classification; dataset quality/leakage, cross-file context, robustness and explainability are the key open challenges.

title: Evaluating large language models for multilingual vulnerability detection at dual granularities
design: Empirical comparison of 8 fine-tuned/embedding PLMs vs 5 LLMs (zero-shot, BM25 few-shot, instruction tuning) at function and line level, 7 languages
dataset: REEF (NVD + Mend CVEs 2016-2023; C, C++, C#, Go, Java, JavaScript, Python), functions ≤512 tokens; plus 2024-2025 time-split and imbalanced variants
sample_size: Function level 20,165 functions (test 2,026, balanced); line level 8,134 vulnerable functions (test 810); imbalanced test 6,051; time-split test 3,138 / 1,328
metrics: Accuracy, precision, recall, F1, FPR, FNR, MCC, AUC (pooled over languages); per-CWE and per-severity correct-detection counts; API/TCO cost
main_finding: Fine-tuned GPT-4o + few-shot beats CodeT5P (acc 0.7196 vs 0.6037; line F1 0.6641 vs 0.4841) on balanced data, but PLMs win on imbalanced data.

title: To Think or Not to Think: Evaluating LLM Reasoning and Agents in Vulnerability Detection
venue: Proceedings of the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering
design: controlled factorial empirical study; 4 open LLMs x instruct/thinking mode x zero/few-shot x NA/SA/DA/MA orchestration (64 configs), call-matched baselines, blinded human + calibrated LLM-judge explanation study
dataset: PrimeVul Pair (C/C++ functions; 870 instances = 435 vulnerable + 435 benign paired functions); 193-pair subset for call-matched runs
sample_size: 870 functions (435 pairs) x 64 configurations; 120 human-rated and 480 judge-rated explanations
metrics: accuracy, precision, recall, F1, pair-wise correct prediction (P-C), FPR, predicted-positive rate, F1 SD/CV; explanation Likert scores; GPU-hours, kWh, tokens, USD
main_finding: Thinking raises non-agent F1 0.31->0.41 (p=0.023) via recall at 2.7-4.4x energy; dual-agent tops F1 by flagging 88.2%; self-revision matches multi-agent pairwise accuracy.

title: A Real CVE-Backed Benchmark for WordPress Plugin Vulnerability Detection: Re-Evaluating Static and Learning-Based Detectors Under Leakage-Controlled Evaluation
design: empirical benchmark; plugin-grouped 5-fold CV (de-duplicated, clone-collapsed) of an in-house static taint analyser vs classical ML and LSTM detectors vs 3 trivial baselines; no LLMs
dataset: new WordPress plugin PHP benchmark from 1757 real CVEs (NVD + cvelistV5), 1281 plugins; function-level diff labels; Variant A (patched-twin negatives) and Variant B (untouched same-plugin negatives)
sample_size: 15,294 (Variant A) and 24,917 (Variant B) PHP functions after leakage control (30,860 each before); 400 functions expert-reviewed
metrics: macro-F1 (fold mean, 95% CI), accuracy, balanced accuracy, MCC, PR-AUC, vulnerable-class FNR, per-class P/R/F1; paired fold- and plugin-level tests with Cohen's d
main_finding: Best binary macro-F1 0.563/0.601; neural models never lead; token-count baseline rivals TF-IDF RF; unnamed intra-procedural lexical taint analyser misses ~98%; 48.8% of cleaned positives genuine.

title: Sifting the Noise: A Comparative Study of LLM Agents in Vulnerability False Positive Filtering
venue: Proceedings of the ACM on Software Engineering
design: Comparative empirical study: 3 LLM agent frameworks x 3 backbones vs vanilla prompting for filtering SAST false positives; ablations + post-cutoff check
dataset: OWASP Benchmark v1.2 (Java, synthetic) with 4 SAST tools; Vul4J real-world Java CodeQL alerts; post-cutoff OSS-Fuzz C/C++ CodeQL alerts
sample_size: OWASP 2,740 cases (1,325 negatives / 1,415 positives); Vul4J 50 sampled alerts (31 FP/19 TP); OSS-Fuzz 50 alerts (22 FP/28 TP)
metrics: residual FPR; FP identification rate (recall), precision, F1, accuracy; TP retention / miss rate; tokens, rounds, USD per task
main_finding: Best agent (SWE-agent+Claude Sonnet 4) cuts OWASP FPR 98.3%->6.3% but suppresses 22.25% of true vulns; gains depend on backbone and CWE.

title: Benchmarking LLMs and LLM-based Agents in Practical Vulnerability Detection for Code Repositories
venue: Proceedings of the 63rd Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers)
design: benchmark paper + comparative evaluation of plain LLM, dependency-augmented LLM and ReAct agent across 4 prompting strategies and 4 foundation models
dataset: JITVul, 879 CVEs from PrimeVul (91 CWEs, C/C++), each target function paired with vulnerability-introducing and vulnerability-fixing commit
sample_size: 1,758 paired samples (879 vulnerable, 879 benign) from 879 CVEs; extra non-paired PrimeVul test set 695 vul / 25,216 benign
metrics: F1, pairwise accuracy (pAcc); share of pairwise error types; tool-invocation counts
main_finding: ReAct agents get best pairwise accuracy but all GPT-4o/4o-mini methods stay at pAcc <=20.17% despite F1 48-66%; F1 is misleading on balanced data.

title: Comparison of Static Application Security Testing Tools and Large Language Models for Repo-level Vulnerability Detection
design: Empirical comparison, 15 SAST tools vs 12 open-source LLMs (fine-tuned + prompted) on repo-level detection; preprint
dataset: Real-world CVE repos: Java (Li et al.), C (Lipp et al.), new Python dataset from NVD
sample_size: 270 CVEs in 134 repos (87 Java, 85 C, 98 Python); ~5.5M functions; random 8:1:1 split, test set roughly 8-10 CVEs per language
metrics: Vulnerability detection ratio (S1 any function, S2 all functions); marked function ratio as FPR proxy; no precision/F1
main_finding: SAST tools detect few vulnerabilities (up to 44.4%) but mark few functions; LLMs detect up to 100% but mark up to 77.4%.

title: Large Language Model for Vulnerability Detection and Repair: Literature Review and the Road Ahead
venue: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
design: Systematic literature review (manual top-venue search + 7-database automated search + snowballing + 5-criterion quality scoring); descriptive mapping, no meta-analysis
dataset: 13 conferences + 4 journals (manual); IEEE Xplore, ACM DL, SpringerLink, Wiley, ScienceDirect, Web of Science, arXiv; Jan 2018 - Mar 2024
sample_size: 58 primary studies (40 detection studies in Table 2, 19 repair studies in Table 3; 1,535 records screened)
metrics: Counts/shares of LLMs used, adaptation techniques, input granularity, data labeling and deployment features across included studies
main_finding: To Mar 2024, LLM vulnerability detection was dominated by fine-tuned small encoder models on function-level, heuristically labelled data; none integrated into developer workflows.
